values.definition: Short, cropped jacket originally designed for Air Force fighter pilots. Defined by elasticated cuffs, collar, and hem, full-zip front, zip pockets including one on the arm, and typically a shiny nylon face fabric. The MA-1 by Alpha Industries is the definitive model. Currently enjoying a renewed spike in popularity.

Cropped jacket usually cut from denim with button front, chest pockets, classic collar, and seam details. Dates back to the late 1800s, originally created for farmers and gold prospectors. Raw denim versions develop unique fades over time. Extremely versatile and timeless.

Lightweight blouson jacket with stand collar, ribbed or tapered waist, and slanted or vertical pockets. Originally the Baracuta G9, created in 1930s Manchester. A pop culture icon worn by Steve McQueen, James Dean, and Elvis Presley. Perfect for transitional weather and smart casual outfits.

Sporty, lightweight jacket designed primarily for wind and light rain protection. Made from thin synthetic fabric, often nylon. A functional transitional jacket brought back into spotlight by the gorpcore trend. Typically features zip front, elastic cuffs, and drawstring hem.

Casual hooded sweatshirt available in pullover and zip-up variants. Made from cotton, fleece, or blended fabrics. Ranges from athletic to streetwear styling. Can be worn as a standalone top or layered under jackets. See hoodie_type parameter for subtypes.

Down-insulated jacket defined by oversized baffles creating a distinctive 'Michelin Man' appearance. First rose to fame in the 1990s. Often features a cropped body and oversized fit. Only works as an outer layer due to bulk. Current trend favors big baffles and cropped cuts.

Military-heritage utilitarian outerwear based on the M-65. Constructed from heavy cotton twill with a funnel collar. Features multiple pockets and a rugged, practical design. Three main variants: military field jacket, barn-style field coat, and motorcycle field jacket. Extremely versatile for layering.

Cropped leather jacket with asymmetric zipper, belted waist, and large collar. First introduced by Schott NYC as the 'Perfecto' in 1928. Popularized by Marlon Brando in The Wild One (1953). A counterculture icon and universal symbol of rebellion. The most recognizable outerwear design.

The oldest and most iconic leather jacket style, originally designed for WWI pilots. Features a relaxed fit, shoulder epaulets, standup collar, front slit or flap pockets, and side zip pockets. Often includes sherpa or shearling collar. Also called flight or aviator jacket.

Sleek leather jacket with minimal embellishments, also called a cafe racer or moto jacket. Features a snap-over band collar, straightforward zip front, and slim fit. A cleaner, more versatile alternative to the biker jacket with a polished aesthetic.

Leather version of the classic denim trucker jacket. Features a waist-length cut, button-flap chest pockets, button front closure, and heavy seam work. Combines the classic trucker silhouette with premium leather for a rugged, elevated look.

Lightweight workwear jacket originating from 1900s France, designed for laborers and artists. Features oversized pockets (at least one chest pocket and larger hip pockets), generous cut for unrestricted movement, and button front. Made from denim, waxed cotton, canvas, or boiled wool.

Lightweight windbreaker-style jacket with snap button closure, originally worn by NFL coaches in the 1990s. Made from thin nylon with a classic collar, slit pockets, elasticated cuffs, and drawstring hem. Moves easily, resists moisture, and goes on/off quickly.

Jacket featuring insulating padding stitched in quilted patterns for lightweight warmth. Less bulky than puffers, with a more tailored appearance. Available in diamond or horizontal quilt patterns. Perfect for layering in transitional weather.

Lightweight zip-front athletic jacket, often with contrast stripes along the sleeves. Typically made from polyester or tricot fabric with a stand-up collar. Originates from sportswear but adopted into casual and retro-inspired street style.

Cropped, boxy jacket originating from US high school and college sports. Traditional version has a wool body with leather sleeves. Modern interpretations use fleece or cotton blends with a trimmer cut. Snap-button front closure with ribbed cuffs, hem, and collar.

Country-heritage jacket made from cotton treated with wax coating (beeswax or paraffin) for water resistance and durability. Develops a unique patina over time. Features storm fly front, corduroy collar, fleece-lined pockets. Best in earthy green and brown. Needs periodic re-waxing.

Farm-heritage jacket built from heavy cotton canvas or waxed cotton with a boxier cut and soft corduroy collar. Features flannel or quilted lining, patch pockets placed lower on the body, and a relaxed fit. A more easy-going, broken-in alternative to the field jacket.

Hybrid garment between a shirt and a jacket, also known as a shirt jacket, shirt jac, or CPO jacket. Provides warmth of a light jacket without bulk. Excellent freedom of movement. Made from cotton blends, flannel, corduroy, or wool. An alternative to a cardigan or hoodie for layering.

Cozy mid-layer jacket primarily designed for insulation, particularly when combined with a shell jacket. Heavy-pile versions (like Patagonia's Retro-X) are popular. Associated with gorpcore trend. Great for adding texture to autumn/winter outfits.

US Air Force-style jacket made from sheepskin with a thick shearling collar. Similar in cut to a bomber but differs in materials and lining. Predates the nylon MA-1 bomber. Provides exceptional warmth and a rugged, heritage aesthetic.

Long, heavily insulated winter coat, often extending to mid-thigh or below. Features a hood (frequently fur-trimmed), multiple pockets, and a drawstring waist. Favored by Arctic explorers and mountaineers. The ultimate winter coat for extreme cold protection.

Pullover-style weatherproof jacket, typically with a half-zip or quarter-zip front and a kangaroo pocket. Lighter than a parka, designed for wind and rain protection. Often features a hood. A practical outdoor and urban option.

parameters.name: hoodie_type
parameters.description: The specific subtype or variation of hoodie, distinguished by closure style, fit, sleeve configuration, and fabric weight

values.definition: Classic collarless, slip-on hooded sweatshirt without a front opening. Often features a kangaroo pocket. Offers more warmth and a cleaner silhouette than zip-up variants. The most traditional hoodie design.

Hoodie with a full-length zipper from hem to collar allowing easy wear and temperature control. Also called a zip-front hoodie. Offers better breathability and layering versatility than pullovers. The most common hoodie closure variant.

Hoodie with a zipper extending from the chest to the collar (approximately half the front). Provides some ventilation control while maintaining a cleaner front aesthetic than a full zip. A sportier, more polished alternative.

Hoodie with a short zipper at the collar for minimal ventilation adjustment. Maintains most of the pullover's clean front appearance while allowing easier on/off. Often seen in athletic and performance styles.
Relaxed, generously cut hoodie with a street-style aesthetic. Often gender-neutral in design. Features dropped shoulders and extra room throughout. Popular in streetwear and athleisure contexts.

Tailored hoodie with a sleek, close-to-body silhouette. Ideal for layering under jackets or for activewear. Available in both pullover and zip-up designs. Creates a more polished appearance than standard-fit hoodies.

Hoodie with sleeves removed for greater arm mobility and ventilation. Provides a more athletic silhouette. Commonly used in training, bodybuilding, and casual streetwear crossover. Often features a half-zip front.

Hoodie made from fleece fabric with a soft brushed interior for excellent insulation. Best for cold weather and lounging. Can pill if low-quality. Available in heavyweight variants for outerwear-level warmth.
Hoodie under 300g/m2 fabric weight. Ideal for spring layering and workouts. Made from thin cotton, cotton-poly blends, or performance fabrics. Not designed as standalone cold-weather wear.
Hoodie at 400g/m2 or above fabric weight. Structured, premium feel perfect for outerwear looks. Provides substantial warmth and body. Often features a more boxy, substantial silhouette.

parameters.name: casual_jacket_formality
parameters.description: The formality range of a casual jacket, indicating the dress codes it can appropriately serve within the casual-to-smart-casual spectrum

values.definition: Jacket suitable exclusively for casual, relaxed settings. Not appropriate for business-casual or smart-casual dress codes. Includes: puffer, anorak, track jacket, hoodie (standard), fleece jacket, parka, sleeveless hoodie. These styles read as athletic, outdoor, or loungewear.

Jacket that spans from casual to smart-casual settings, versatile enough to pair with both t-shirts/jeans and chinos/button-downs. Includes: bomber, denim trucker, harrington, field jacket, chore coat, barn jacket, coach jacket, waxed jacket, shacket/overshirt, quilted jacket, varsity. These styles can be dressed up or down depending on what is worn underneath.

Jacket that leans toward the dressier end of casual outerwear, suitable for smart-casual occasions and can sometimes work for informal business settings. Includes: leather racer/cafe racer, leather bomber (quality versions), suede bomber, harrington (in premium fabrics). These styles pair well with dress shirts, tailored trousers, and loafers.

parameters.name: leather_jacket_subtype
parameters.description: The specific subtype of leather jacket based on design origin, silhouette, and closure style

values.definition: The iconic double-rider jacket with an asymmetric front zipper, belted waist, wide lapels/collar, and cropped length. First produced by Schott NYC in 1928. Double layer of front material for insulation. The most recognizable leather jacket style and a symbol of rebellion.

Clean, minimalist leather jacket with a snap-over band collar, simple zip front, and slim fit. Few embellishments for a polished, versatile look. Named after 1960s British motorcycle culture. The most versatile leather jacket style for everyday wear.

Relaxed-fit leather jacket inspired by WWI pilot gear. Features shoulder epaulets, standup collar, front slit or flap pockets, side zip pockets. Often with sherpa or shearling collar. The oldest leather jacket style.

Sheepskin leather jacket with thick shearling wool lining visible at the collar, cuffs, and sometimes the hem. Inspired by WWII Air Force jackets. Provides exceptional warmth. A heritage style combining rugged leather with luxurious wool.

Leather interpretation of the classic denim trucker jacket silhouette. Waist-length cut with button-flap chest pockets, button front, and heavy seam work. Combines workwear heritage with leather's premium feel.

Military-inspired leather jacket with the practical, multi-pocket design of a field jacket rendered in premium leather. Features funnel collar and utilitarian pocket placement. Looks sharp paired with slacks and tucked-in shirts.

Structured leather jacket cut in a blazer silhouette with notch lapels and button front. Bridges the gap between casual leather and tailored clothing. A refined option for smart-casual to semi-formal settings. Shearling versions available for added warmth.

garment_harmony_principles.name: width_harmony_rule
garment_harmony_principles.description: Tie width, lapel width, and collar spread should be approximately equal for visual balance

garment_harmony_principles.name: collar_face_matching
garment_harmony_principles.description: Collar style should complement face shape: spread collars widen narrow faces, point collars narrow wide faces. Collar height should match neck length. Small collars make large heads appear larger.
garment_harmony_principles.note: D04 defines garment capability (e.g., 'spread collar achieves widening visual effect'). D01 defines body requirement (e.g., 'wide face needs narrowing collar'). The mapping between them is via cross_domain_dependencies.

garment_harmony_principles.name: knot_collar_fill
garment_harmony_principles.description: The tie knot should fill the collar opening appropriately — outer borders of the knot should correspond with inner borders of the collar points.

garment_harmony_principles.name: formality_consistency
garment_harmony_principles.summary: All ensemble elements should be at roughly the same formality level. See D06 for the canonical formality_consistency principle.

garment_harmony_principles.name: showing_linen_principle
garment_harmony_principles.description: The shirt collar should sit above the jacket collar (showing 1/2 inch) and shirt cuffs should show 1/2 to 3/4 inch below jacket sleeves. These are two of Flusser's five critical body intersections.

garment_harmony_principles.name: trouser_jacket_balance
garment_harmony_principles.description: Trouser rise must be high enough that the waistband sits at or near the natural waist for ideal visual balance between jacket and trousers. Low-rise trousers doom this balance.

garment_harmony_principles.name: stripe_elongation_effect
garment_harmony_principles.description: Vertical elements (stripes, side vents, hacking pockets, peak lapels) create illusion of height. Horizontal elements (cuffs, wide lapels, pocket flaps, double-breasted closure) add visual width.
